Quiz

When someone becomes
a Christian, we say they…

A.Get saved
B.Accept Christ
C.Obey the gospel
From quizzes.md. Answer: C (say it; no click). Let the room argue first. “Obey the gospel” is Walter Scott’s language, and Raines’s: “I can see no way out, with the Word of God in my hand, but through the obedience of faith in baptism.” Hold it: which gospel, and how did they hear it? We come back to it at the end.
Our Wild Democracy · Chapter 9

The Tale of a
Young Universalist

Aylett Raines, Walter Scott and the Campbells · 1828
Chapter 9. Last week: Lexington, where they united on the Bible and not on their readings of it. This morning: how did they read it? A story about a man who came to argue and could not.
Points of contention
Trinity
Atonement
Clergy
Communion
Baptism
Future
Six clicks, one line each. Atonement: how Christ saves (Stone rejected the substitutionary “satisfaction” view; Smith at Lexington names “the Ground and Nature of the Atonement” with the Trinity). Side by side, as we tell it: Trinity, Christ: the Christians kept to Scripture’s words, and to the Reformers looked “Arian”; the Reformers held the Trinitarian faith. Trinity, the Spirit: the Christians, that he works directly, in conversion and revival (the camp meeting, the anxious seat); the Reformers, that he works through the word (believe the gospel facts, confess, be immersed). Clergy: ordained elders and preachers serve the ordinances, or any disciple may, the church appointing. Table: free communion or restricted to the immersed; now and then, or every Lord’s day. Baptism: immersion, but not “for the remission of sins,” or immersion for the remission of sins. Future: Christ comes first, to judge, or the gospel brings the millennium. Williams, p. 450: “some of each party still cherished honest doubts respecting the doctrine of the others.” Christ and the Spirit, Williams, p. 450: “Some Reformers still looked upon the Christians as Arians; and some Christians were adverse to the union, in the belief that the Reformers denied the influence of the Spirit, and attached undue importance to baptism.” The Spirit here is his work in conversion (Campbell: the Spirit works through the word), not his place in the Trinity. Baptism: “all did not hold in the same sense that baptism was for the remission of sins.” Most Christians had come to immerse; Stone: the Reformers “preached baptism for the remission of sins to believing penitents.” The table: “they still differed on the question of free or restricted communion”; Stone: the Reformers “insisted also upon weekly communion, which we had neglected” (Biography). Clergy: Stone, 1830: “the church may elect, but not ordain”; Campbell: any disciple may break the loaf; the Lexington churches split on exactly this in February 1832. Conversion: Stone’s revival culture (Cane Ridge) against Scott’s plan of salvation (believe, repent, be baptized, receive). The future: Stone premillennial by 1832–33; Campbell postmillennial (Chapter 7). These are generalizations: people on both sides held both views on several points.
The handshake
Stained-glass window, Cane Ridge Meeting House (photograph: therestorationmovement.com)
Over an open Bible on the pulpit; the communion table before them, two plates and two cups. Set it against Marburg: Luther would not take the hand; Stone offered his. Maker and date of the window: unknown (to find). Class use only.
Handshake by handshake
Person by person
Congregation by congregation
Three clicks. Then the maps. As it spread: 1832, Smith (a Disciple) and Rogers (a Christian) ride together to every church; 1832, Smith defends himself to his own alarmed Reformers; 1834, Jacksonville, Illinois: Stone joins neither church until they unite; 1835, Lexington, at last. Stone at Jacksonville: “I refused to unite with either until they united together, and labored to effect it. It was effected” (Biography, p. 79). Where it was slow, Stone blamed “a few ignorant, headstrong bigots on both sides.”
The union spreading, 1831–1835
Six clicks: five waves of union, then the refusals. From the database’s Gazetteer of Local Unions (36 dated unions, 15 refusals; places approximate). (1) Georgetown in the autumn of 1831, the handshake at Lexington; already, unprompted, Rush County, Indiana (“The Reforming Baptists and we, are all one here,” Dec. 1831) and Maury County, Tennessee. Stone and Johnson: “The spirit of union is spreading like fire in dry stubble.” (2) 1832: Paris, Millersburg, Carlisle (Smith’s letter), Montgomery and Bath counties, Republican (500 break the loaf), Pendleton County (“a union of all present took place”), Calloway County, McNairy County and Lock’s Creek in Tennessee. (3) Autumn 1832: the yearly meeting at Clintonville; Stone in Illinois: “a happy union of the two societies, Christians and Reformers, in one body or church” at Jacksonville; Carrollton, Jersey Prairie; Troy, Missouri. (4) 1833–34: Bowling Green and Fayette, Missouri; White River and Silver Creek, Indiana; Paris enrols as one church (Aug. 1834); Jacksonville, where Stone in 1834 found two churches again and would join neither “until they united together.” (5) July 1835: Lexington itself, at last. (6) Refused: Liberty, Indiana (1841: “we no longer seek for union with the Disciples”), Preble County, Ohio; Purviance’s Ohio churches; the eastern Christian Connection. About half of Stone’s Christians never entered the union (Encyclopedia, “Christian Connection”). Stone, 1835: “we have had no general council on this subject. Churches have acted in their private capacity.”
If asked what became of those who refused (only if it comes up): the Christian Connection merged with the Congregationalists (1931), then into the United Church of Christ (1957). The Disciples and the UCC: “Declaration of Ecumenical Partnership” (1985), “full communion” (1989), after the Disciples recognized infant baptism as “a legitimate form of baptism” (1987). Recognition, not agreement. The UCC receives the creeds “as testimonies, but not tests of the faith.” (Encyclopedia; ucc.org.)
One movement, spreading · 1836–1860
Five clicks. The map opens with the unions of 1831–35 already lit. After 1836 the record shows no new unions of Christians and Disciples, only refusals (the Gazetteer of Local Unions); what spreads is the one movement. Each light is the earliest report found in the Millennial Harbinger (pages from the OCR, approximate). (1) Already, beyond the union, the Campbells’ Reformers: the Western Reserve (Scott, 1827–28); Pittsburgh, Philadelphia (Bank Street, 1832), New York (1834), eastern Virginia (1832), Little Rock (1832: the Philadelphia Confession “renounced by the church”), Alabama (1833–34), Toronto (1834: “a little band of reformers… about twenty in number”). (2) 1836–39: near Dubuque, 1 Nov. 1835, a church “of eight members” (MH 1836, p. 88); Middleville, Michigan, “a company of disciples in this place” (1836); Clarke County, Georgia (1836); Mississippi (1836); Grant County, Wisconsin: “We met on the second Lord’s day in October, when eleven of us united together” (1838; MH 1839); Saint John, New Brunswick (1839); Nottingham, “a congregation of New Testament Disciples” (MH 1837), and New Mills near Glasgow (1837). (3) 1840–47: Little Rock and Fayetteville (1840); Texas, Gay Hill (1841) and Bowie County, “constituted a church of sixteen members” (MH 1842); Hookerton, North Carolina: “between twenty and thirty churches” (MH 1845); Oregon, Yamhill: “in March we organized a congregation upon the Book alone”, the first in the Territory (1846, letter in MH 1848, p. 402). (4) 1852–57: “In Stockton and San Jose there are churches. In Stockton the brethren meet weekly to break the loaf” (MH 1852); Kansas Territory, Timbered Hill (1856) and Leavenworth (1857); Sydney, Australia (MH 1852). (5) Their own estimates, not counts: “at least one hundred thousand” (MH 1839); “two hundred thousand soldiers of the Cross” (MH 1848); 1860: “nearly one hundred churches in Great Britain”, “in the United States upwards of 300,000 brethren”, and Australia (MH 1860). The Harbinger itself doubted the larger figures (1857: “This may be too large a figure”). Nebraska: no congregation reported by 1860.

Opens where the last map ended: its dots (the union, 1831–35, and the first reports to 1860) stay on throughout. Eleven clicks: 1850, 1860, 1870, 1906, 1926, 1940, 1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, 2000 (the map stops at 2000; 2020: 3,253,056 adherents, 19,978 congregations, for the notes only). 1940–1970 are not counts: each county is eased in a straight line from 1926 to 1980, to carry the picture through the decades the surveys miss. Each glow grows with the number of people (before 1906, churches) in that county. An illustration, not a data display: where a county is lit before and after a year but blank in it, the gap is filled by interpolating between the two (this fills the states missing from the 1870 file). 1850–1870: the decennial census counted churches and their seats by denomination, and its category “Christian” took in both the Disciples and the Christian Connection (the Christians who never united), so those three frames are churches of both, each glow sized by the number of churches (IPUMS NHGIS, county tables). The 1870 file is incomplete: New York, Pennsylvania, Michigan, New Jersey and Wisconsin have no “Christian” figures at all (they had 102, 69, 13, 10 and 8 churches in 1860), so the Northeast looks emptier than it was; where the data are complete, 1860–1870 is growth (Ohio 365 to 681 churches, Kentucky 304 to 490, Missouri 150 to 393, Illinois 148 to 350). From 1906, people: members in the U.S. Census of Religious Bodies (1906, 1926), adherents (members plus children and others attending) from 1980; so the step from 1926 to 1980 is partly a change of measure. 1906 was the first census to count the Disciples and the Churches of Christ apart (the division made official). 1926 is the high point of the old census; the Depression-era 1936 census undercounted and is left out. The Christian Churches and Churches of Christ appear separately from 1971. About 2%% of each year could not be placed by county (renamed or vanished counties; Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico); the totals in the captions are the full totals from each file. Congregations: about 12,300 surviving 1926 schedules; 22,336 (1980); 21,936 (2000); 19,978 (2020). Sources: IPUMS NHGIS (Schroeder et al., version 21.0, 2026, doi:10.18128/D050.V21.0), 1850, 1860, 1870 county church tables; United States Census of Religious Bodies, County File, 1906 and 1926 (ARDA, from ICPSR 8); Churches and Church Membership in the United States, 1980 and Religious Congregations and Membership Study, 2000 (ARDA county files); 2020 U.S. Religion Census (ASARB, 2022). Figures are as each body reported them.

This time

A young
Universalist.

This time: a Universalist preacher comes to heckle Walter Scott, and stays. Aylett Raines, the Western Reserve, 1828.
Our man

Aylett Raines

Born in Virginia, 1797 or 1798. Five years a Universalist preacher.
A reconstruction: Raines at about thirty, in 1828
The face is a modern reconstruction of Raines at about thirty, worked from his one known photograph, taken late in life (images/SOURCES.md); not a period likeness, so say so. Restorationist: a Universalist who held there is punishment after death, and then all are restored (Winchester’s Dialogues, the book that converted him). Hayden: born near Fredericksburg, Spotsylvania County (p. 150, “1797”; his gravestone, as reported online, 22 Jan. 1798: to check). Christened at four in the Episcopal church, “amidst many tears,” tears “of fear and apprehension” (Hayden’s words). Skeptical in his teens, after contradictory preaching and Paine’s Age of Reason. Teaching school near Fredonia, Indiana, his employers were Universalists; he lost the arguments, and Winchester “completed the work.” Died at Eminence, Kentucky, 1881 (to check); fifty years a preacher of the gospel in Ohio and Kentucky.
His road: Virginia; at fourteen, Jefferson County, Kentucky; teaching near Fredonia, Indiana, where he became a Universalist; then two years preaching “at large,” which brought him to the Western Reserve in 1828. Map drawn for the class from U.S. Census boundaries; the Reserve is shaded by today’s counties.
Elsewhere, a Universalist asks to be immersed

“He had, therefore, offered to receive it by the hands of both Baptist and Methodist, but neither would baptize him unless he would renounce his faith in Universal Salvation.”

Nathaniel Stacy, on Cornelius G. Person, New York, 1817 · in Eddy, Universalism in America, vol. 2, p. 7
• Person, a Universalist preacher in Greenfield, N.Y., came to believe he should be immersed; he “considered all who named the name of Christ as Christians.” Refused by both, he asked Stacy, a fellow Universalist, who came the next February: “we had a hole cut in the ice, and I baptized him” (Eddy II, 8). The contrast with Warren: the Baptists and Methodists asked him to give up the opinion first; the Mahoning Association, itself still a Baptist association in 1828, received Raines with his opinion kept as private property.
Raines, on becoming a Universalist

“I got religion. The sky appeared to be bluer, the leaves looked greener, and the birds sang more sweetly than ever before.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 151
• He goes on: “I underwent a great moral change. There was much of the love of God in it. Shrouded as I was in error, yet there were apertures through which the love of God passed into my heart, and made me inexpressibly happy.” Then: “I now commenced the study of the Scriptures in good earnest, and after two years commenced preaching.” He preached Restorationism “five years.” A real conversion, in his own telling, to a faith he would later leave.
His debates

“In these, one sectarianism was arrayed against another; and those that came plunging and crashing against mine seemed so very frail, and made so feeble a defense, as rather to confirm me in my errors.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 151
• Five years a Universalist preacher, two of them traveling “at large”: “This, of course, provoked great opposition, and I had a number of debates.” Argument only confirmed him. Hold that against what Scott does.
The Western Reserve: Connecticut’s strip of northeast Ohio, kept when it ceded its western claims (1786), sold in 1795, surveyed in 1796, and settled by New Englanders, who brought Universalism with them. Everything in this story happens within about thirty miles: Windham, Ravenna, Shalersville, Sandy Lake, Austintown, Warren. New Lisbon, where Walter Scott first preached the “ancient gospel” (November 1827), lies south of the Reserve; Bethany, the Campbells’ home, seventy miles south. The Mahoning Baptist Association had made Scott its evangelist in 1827; by August 1828 nearly a thousand had been added to its churches (Richardson II, p. 244).
The Reserve in 1828

“Misrepresentations… were as numerous as blackbirds in August…”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 152
• In full: “Hundreds were being baptized. Much interest had been awakened in behalf of the gospel, and bitter was the opposition which had been enlisted against it. Misrepresentations — not to use a harsher term — were as numerous as blackbirds in August, and these too, very often by those who professed to be ‘embassadors for Christ’”. The rumor about Scott’s preaching: “Just say you believe, and let a preacher dip you”.
Windham, 1828

Walter Scott

The evangelist of the Mahoning Association, 1827–30.
Scott (1796–1861): Scottish-born, a schoolmaster in Pittsburgh, the Association’s evangelist from August 1827. His plan of the gospel in “six points” (later counted on five fingers): faith, repentance, baptism, remission of sins, the gift of the Holy Spirit, eternal life. He was known to call for objections at the end of a sermon.
He came to argue

“…I had been told that he was a very bold man, and at the close of his discourses he challenged objectors to make known their objections. Here, thought I, will be a good opportunity for me! and hence I let a number of my brethren know that I intended to oppose him.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 152
• At Samuel Robbins’s house, in the town of Windham, at night. Richardson (II, p. 220): Raines “did not believe in water baptism, but in the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost,” and “expected to have a discussion with him.”
The first night

“…when he called for objections I was confounded. I could see the heads of my brethren moving to the right and left, in the crowd, expecting to see me rise to my feet. But they didn’t see me rise!”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 152
• Scott read 1 Corinthians 1 and “preached it through, not forgetting to state and defend what he styled the six points of the gospel. I was greatly surprised.” Why he kept his seat: “I felt certain that if I opposed Bro. Scott I would expose myself. His discourse appeared to me, at every point, invulnerable.” Richardson: he was even asked to close the meeting in prayer, and slipped in his favorite petition, for “a Pentecostean season” and the baptism “with fire” (II, p. 220).
Why he kept his seat

“I felt certain that if I opposed Bro. Scott I would expose myself. His discourse appeared to me, at every point, invulnerable.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), pp. 152–153
• Scott had not argued with him. He read a chapter and preached it through.
Asked to close in prayer

“…when called upon to close the meeting, made an excellent prayer, desiring that all might have a spirit of obedience, etc., but taking care to introduce his favorite petition that they might have a Pentecostean season and be baptized with the Holy Ghost and with fire.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell, vol. 2 (1870), p. 220
• Richardson’s telling, not Raines’s own words. The heckler, asked to pray, got his objection in anyway: the Universalists held to the baptism of fire and the Spirit, not of water. Next day he went back, “hoping that he would now be more successful in detecting errors” (p. 220).
Outside, in the yard
His brethren: “Bro. Raines, what do you think of the discourse?”
Raines: “I can do nothing against the gospel as preached by Bro. Scott; unless I should live to disgrace it; which may our gracious Lord forbid!”
Two clicks. Raines, 1868, Hayden p. 153. He adds: “Hence I have no sympathy with those who say they can not understand the preachers of the reformation. I understood the first I ever heard a great deal better than I desired.” (That line next.)
Raines

“I understood the first I ever heard a great deal better than I desired.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 153
• The laugh line. Then he went back the next night.
Four nights

He kept coming back

1 Corinthians 1: the points of the gospel.
1 Corinthians 15: the resurrection.
The two covenants: the old and the new.
Hebrews 11: the story of faith.
Four clicks. Each is a whole chapter or a whole sweep of Scripture, not a verse. Richardson: Scott “was accustomed to take the Scriptures connectedly” (II, p. 221).
His proof-text

“As in Adam all die, even so in Christ
shall all be made alive.”

1 Corinthians 15:22, Raines’s own proof-text. Raines: “I deemed a passage of cardinal importance, and the whole chapter very good in its place; but as I did not understand it, of course I saw none of its beauties, and was superlatively ignorant of the meaning of the scrap just referred to, which was one of the proof-texts by which I attempted to prove the ultimate holiness and happiness of all men” (Hayden p. 153). Richardson: Universalist preachers had little use for the chapter “with the exception of a single sentence in it” (II, p. 221).
The second night: the resurrection

“Germs of truth, and beauties and glories sprang from the bosom of that chapter under the handling of Bro Scott, of which before I had scarcely any conception.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 153
• The same chapter he had quoted for years, read whole. Richardson: under Scott, the chapter “soon presented itself to Mr. Raines as a thing of life, and made to him a revelation of such lofty trains of thought and unspeakable glories that his heart was touched” (II, p. 221).
The resurrection sermon, as Rogers heard it told
Scott: “Brother Rains, is not this so?”
Raines: “I presume it is so.”
Two clicks. Rogers’s telling, from fireside conversations with Raines late in life (Recollections of Men of Faith, 1889): a great meeting, 1 Corinthians 15 all day, Raines sent by his brethren to take notes and seated right before the speaker. An hour in, Scott drove home a passage against Restorationism, then pointed at him. Raines was “afraid to say yes, lest Scott might reply, Then why not come over on our side? He was afraid to say no, lest he might be challenged for a discussion.” Rogers’s scene is bigger than Raines’s own (a night meeting at Robbins’s house, Hayden p. 152); it may be a later day of the same weeks, or memory folding them together. Say so.
His notes

“I have never in all my life heard just such a speaker, or just such preaching. I am sure the preacher is not inspired, but there is inspiration in what he says… He interprets the Word of God after a new fashion… I must think on these things.”

Raines to his brethren, holding up a blank sheet: “Here are my notes, all of them.” · as W. C. Rogers, Recollections of Men of Faith (1889), pp. 30–52, from conversations with Raines
• In full: “I am not now prepared to deny what he says, nor am I ready to accept all. He interprets the Word of God after a new fashion. I tell you the truth. I have so far been unable to detect the slightest flaw in any of his arguments. I must think on these things.” Rogers: “This was a damper to his dear brethren.” Rogers’s report of Raines, not Raines’s pen; checked against a web transcription of the 1889 book, not yet a page scan.
The embrace

“Come, Brother Rains, and preach with me the everlasting gospel to the inhabitants of earth.”

Walter Scott, that evening, coming up from the water in his wet clothes · as W. C. Rogers, Recollections of Men of Faith (1889), pp. 30–52, from conversations with Raines
• Rogers: that evening some were baptized in a stream between high banks. Raines stood alone on the path and lingered, “as if spell-bound.” Scott came up the path in his wet clothes, straight toward him; Raines stepped aside and turned his back, “when Elder Scott rushed upon him, exclaiming, as he embraced him…” Then: “An electric shock could not have thrilled him more. He made no reply.” Scott went to a nearby house and changed. If the meetings were Windham in February 1828, compare Robbins’s diary for February 27: “Ice a foot thick… the first immersion in Windham” (Hayden p. 144). The embrace does what Scott’s preaching did: no argument, an invitation.
The third night: the two covenants

“…although I had been a preacher five years, I certainly did not know the difference between the old covenant and the new. I obtained from them a sort of hotch-potch; or rather I made of them a chaos, and preached the darkness that was on the face of the deep!”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 153
• Genesis 1:2, turned on himself. The old covenant and the new as two acts of one story, told in order. Keep this line: it comes back with Wright.
The fourth night: Hebrews 11

“Here I virtually surrendered — not that I was convinced that all men would not be finally saved.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 154
• Scott “still bore himself aloft in all the grandeur of the gospel, and in the captivating intelligence of the truth as it is in Jesus.” Note what did not happen: Scott did not argue him out of his Universalism. Next slide.
What Scott said about his Universalism

“Bro. Scott said nothing on this subject, only that it was a philosophy, as was Calvinism, Arminianism, etc., and no part of Christianity.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 154
• Raines goes on: “He convinced me that I ought to lay my philosophy aside, and preach the gospel as the apostles preached… This was, so far, a capital conquest, for it terminated in due time in the conviction, in my mind, that Restorationism itself… is founded in error.” Scott set the opinion to one side and preached the story.
Lay it aside

“He convinced me that I ought to lay my philosophy aside, and preach the gospel as the apostles preached, making their discourses a model to be accurately copied by me in all my ministrations.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 154
• Then: “This was, so far, a capital conquest, for it terminated in due time in the conviction, in my mind, that Restorationism itself, as much as I had formerly idolized it, is founded in error.” Not argued out of the opinion: asked to set it aside, and the opinion faded on its own.
The heckler invites hecklers

“I resolved that I would preach as Bro. Scott had done, and as I believed the apostles did, and that at the close of each discourse I would call for objections.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 154
• He had his own preaching tour to finish. “And I told my old brethren that I threw myself on their mercy; in other words, that if they believed me to be going astray, in mercy to set me right. This attempt was often made within this tour, but it only served to convince me more satisfactorily that I was right.” Richardson: their arguments “were so feeble that he became only the more convinced” (II, p. 221).
He tells his own people

“My friends, I find myself in a strait; I am shut up in a dilemma; and I can see no way out, with the Word of God in my hand, but through the obedience of faith in baptism. If any of you can see any other, I implore you in the name of my Master to show it to me.”

Raines at Austintown, April (1828) · as Hayden reports it, p. 131
• He kept his old appointments, and told them so: “I threw myself on their mercy; in other words, that if they believed me to be going astray, in mercy to set me right” (p. 154). At Austintown, word had gone round that he would preach his renunciation of Universalism; the house was full. Hayden: the Universalists “jerked up their chairs, started over the benches, and hurried to their homes.” (Hayden gives “April,” no year; 1828 by the order of events.)
Ebenezer Williams’s town

Ravenna

View in Ravenna · Henry Howe, Historical Collections of Ohio (1847)
Howe’s view of Ravenna in the 1840s; by the image researcher’s reading of Howe’s text, the church shown is the Universalist church (to confirm). Williams: born at Warwick, Mass., 1793; settled in Ravenna in 1815; ordained “minister at large” by the Universalian Association in 1821; preaching at Shalersville a quarter of his time “at one hundred dollars.” In May 1828 he preached there against baptism, from Acts 2, and rode home unhappy: “My text… were constantly occupying my mind” (Hayden pp. 155–156). Then Raines appeared at his door.
Sandy Lake, May 1828

“…taking hold of each other’s hands, we walked into the water. I baptized him; he in turn baptized me. I think they were all Universalists who witnessed the scene. Some cried, some scolded.”

Ebenezer Williams, Universalist preacher of Ravenna · in Hayden, p. 157
• Williams, the minister ordained by the Universalian Association in 1821, had just preached against baptism at Shalersville and could not sleep. Then: “a child came and informed me that Bro. Raines was at the house… Bro. Raines said he had been hearing Walter Scott; that he had got into trouble, and wanted me to help him out” (p. 156). Sandy Lake: “a beautiful pond in the corners of Brimfield and Rootstown.” It cost Williams his salary: “Thus I turned my back on the four hundred a year.” Raines: “within five weeks I immersed fifty persons, three of them, counting Bro. Williams, talented [Universalist] preachers” (p. 154).
The question
1.How did they unite around the Bible?
2.What made Scott’s preaching so compelling?
The end of the Windham story. Hold the question: question 1 was last week’s, still open.
On the road, summer 1828

Thomas Campbell

Sixty-five, a Calvinist all his life.
The author of the Declaration and Address (1809), now on the Western Reserve helping the work. Hayden: “probably no man within the reformation who possessed such authority of personal influence; of noble mien and manly form; grave and serene of countenance” (p. 149).
Raines, on Thomas Campbell

“He interested himself in my favor, and had me travel and preach with him several months… By day and by night, publicly and from house to house, he was my teacher.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), pp. 149–150
• Before: “Not long after this period I made the acquaintance of Bro. Thomas Campbell.” “This I view as a merciful interposition of my Heavenly Father.”
What Raines saw

“Often have I seen him, when he had no reason to believe that any eye saw him but that eye before which all things are naked and open, in his closet, prostrate on his face, pouring out his soul in prayer to God.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 150
• “Not only by word, but by example, he deeply impressed my warm and susceptible heart. He was, emphatically, a godly man.”

A Calvinist and a Universalist,
on the road together.

An old Calvinist and a young Universalist, travelling and preaching for months. They disagreed about the end of all things, and Thomas never set out to argue him out of it. Thomas, in Raines’s memory: “we have mutually unbosomed ourselves to each other.”
The worry

“It was feared that they were, after all, merely baptized Universalists. If this was all, it was nothing.”

A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 158
• Hayden goes on: “Baptized Universalism is Universalism still; not the gospel.” There were “out-of-door discussions touching the prudence of such a loose proceeding” (p. 163). Richardson: some “doubted whether under such circumstances Mr. Raines could be received” (II, p. 244).
In the street at Warren
Dr. Wright: “I understand that you sometimes tell people that you still believe that all men will finally become holy and happy.”
Raines: “I do, sir.”
Dr. Wright: “What then will you do with this passage: These shall go away into everlasting punishment…?”
Raines: “I will not do any thing with it. If I argue with you in defense of my opinions I shall make myself a factionist… and if you get up an argument with me, be careful, you will make yourself a factionist.”
Saturday morning of the Association, after Campbell’s Friday sermon (shown here before it, in the run-through order). Four clicks. Raines, 1868, Hayden pp. 167–168. Matthew 25:46. Raines will not trade proof-texts: to press an opinion is to make a faction. The doctor’s name was Wright. Remember it.
In the street at Warren
Dr. Wright: “Well, sir, I’ll see whether this association will fellowship men of your views.”
Raines: “I will show you that I will have Thomas Campbell, A. Campbell, Walter Scott, Bentley, and a number of others on my side.”
Dr. Wright: “It is impossible.”
Raines: “Well, try it.”
Four clicks. Hayden p. 168. Raines (paraphrasing the first line): “the Doctor, seeing that I was not in his trap, became excited.”
The trial

Warren, August 1828

Public Square, Warren · Henry Howe, Historical Collections of Ohio (1847)
The Mahoning Association met at Warren, the seat of Trumbull County, in the last week of August 1828 (exact days to check). Hayden was there “from first to last” (p. 161). A triumphant meeting: Methodists, Baptists, Universalists, now one body: “a grand demonstration of the possibility of the union of Christians on original Bible ground” (p. 162). And a worry. Engraving from Howe’s drawings of the 1840s, the nearest view we have to the town of 1828.
Raines

“I went to that association expecting trouble… But I resolved to breast the storm.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 167
• In full: “for, although I did not preach my [Universalist] opinions, yet I sometimes told such persons as approached me becomingly, that it was still my opinion that all men would, ultimately, in some distant period of eternity, be saved. Out of this the trouble was to grow.”
Friday: the opening sermon

“Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but without regard to differences of opinion.”

Romans 14:1, in Campbell’s translation · Alexander Campbell’s text at Warren, Friday
• Raines heard Alexander Campbell that day for the first time. “Bro. Campbell dilated lucidly, showing the difference between faith and opinion… I felt very much strengthened and comforted, knowing, if my case came up in the association, I would have at least Bro. Campbell on my side” (Hayden p. 167). Richardson: “As Mr. Campbell was aware of this state of feeling, he took as the subject of his introductory discourse the fourteenth chapter of Romans” (II, p. 244). The sermon’s substance comes back in a moment.

Saturday afternoon:
the case is called.

Not Dr. Wright but Jacob Osborne, “very lugubriously” (Raines), brought it before the Association. Hayden calls him “the careful and judicious Osborne,” pressed by others to have the matter settled. Some were for rejecting Raines, many in doubt, “the greater number” for him (p. 166).
Thomas Campbell rises first

“The devil has brought this question into this association to sow discord among brethren.”

Thomas Campbell, as Raines remembered it · Hayden, p. 168
• Raines (1868): “Bro. Thomas Campbell first responded, as nearly as I can recollect, in words following.” Richardson, more decorously: “such a question was only calculated to create discord among the brethren” (II, p. 245). Alexander Campbell’s own account (1830) does not give the speech.
Thomas Campbell

“Bro. Raines and I have been much together for the last several months, and we have mutually unbosomed ourselves to each other. I am a Calvinist, and he a [Universalist]; and, although I am a Calvinist, I would put my right arm into the fire and have it burnt off before I would raise my hand against him.”

Thomas Campbell, as Raines remembered it · Hayden, p. 168
• Checked by eye: the scan splits “Calvin ist” across a line. Richardson’s version: “He is philosophically a [Universalist] and I am a Calvinist, but notwithstanding this difference of opinion between us, I would put my right hand into the fire and have it burnt off before I would hold up my hands against him” (II, p. 245). “Raise my hand”: they voted by show of hands.
Thomas Campbell

“And if I were Paul, I would have Bro. Raines… to be my Timothy.”

Thomas Campbell, as Raines remembered it · Hayden, p. 168
• Raines answered him two years later, in a letter (coming up): “if I were Timothy, father Campbell should, in preference to any man, be my Paul.”
Walter Scott

“I think… that Bro. Raines has been very badly treated, and I fear that when he speaks he will speak with too much severity.”

Walter Scott, as Raines remembered it · Hayden, p. 168
• Scott: he “concurred with the preceding speakers, and would not have said any thing on the occasion but to give me time for reflection.” Scott buying him a minute to cool down.
Saturday afternoon

Alexander Campbell

Forty years old. His proposal.
Then Alexander rose, and “substantially repeated what he had said in his introductory discourse, on the difference between faith and opinion” (Raines, Hayden p. 168). What was that discourse?
On the bench

“…Bro. Campbell requested me to stand upon a bench, and proclaim to the large concourse present, my own views of my obligations as a Christian and as a preacher of the gospel.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 168
• Hayden’s footnote: “The better to be heard, the house being very full.” What Raines said: “That my Restorationism was a philosophy. That I would neither preach it nor contend for it, but would preach the whole gospel, and teach the whole truth of Christianity according to my best ability.”
The question
Alexander Campbell: “Whether there was any law of Christ by which I could be condemned?”
The Association: “The vote was in the negative, and in my favor by an overwhelming majority.”
Two clicks. Raines, Hayden p. 169. Richardson: “Whether there was any law of Christ by which a brother could be condemned who deported himself as Mr. Raines proposed to do?” decided “by a very large majority” (II, p. 246). Raines: “This I took to be quite a triumph; but the end was not yet.”
Sunday, the sunrise prayer meeting
An old brother: “Brethren, I understand there are certain persons in the fellowship of this association who deny that sinners are saved by grace… I move that such persons be disfellowshiped.”
Raines: “I second that motion; for by grace are ye saved through faith… Now, if any member of this association holds any doctrine contradictory to the teaching of this passage, I move that he be immediately disfellowshiped.”
Raines: “The old Brother who had put the motion, struck a direct line for the door, and the congregation followed him; and there my association troubles ended.”
Three clicks. Hayden p. 169. “In a twinkling I was on my feet.” Ephesians 2:8–9. Raines: “Affairs, however, would probably have taken a very different turn, had somebody else than myself seconded the old man’s motion.”
Some walked away

“…so much dissatisfied were some who had come to the meeting with a view of uniting with the reformers that they declined doing so.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell, vol. 2 (1870), p. 246
• Richardson, on the same page: some of Campbell’s own associates “thought he had in some measure compromised the principle of the Reformation itself.” And the minority stayed so disturbed that “nothing but his prudence and careful avoidance of any effort to teach his speculative opinions prevented a schism.”
Richardson’s verdict

“It gave an example, however, of a freedom of thought of which the religious community had never dreamed…”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell, vol. 2 (1870), p. 247
• The sentence goes on: “and presented in a very striking light the liberality of the basis of Christian union advocated by Mr. Campbell.” His reasoning just before: Raines believed God “would reward the righteous and punish the wicked according to their works”; that was the substance of the revelation, and anything beyond it “mere opinions or speculations.”
The question
1.How did they unite around the Bible?
2.What made Scott’s preaching so compelling?
3.How could the Campbells embrace a Universalist?
Hold it. Campbell’s own reasons come at the end, after Wright.
Up all night

“His main object was to convince the people that God meant what he said in his Word, which caused great excitement… many sitting up all night reading the Scriptures to see if they meant what they said…”

Samuel Robbins’s diary, Braceville Ridge, February 23, 1828 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 143
• Scott preaching, the winter before Warren; the excitement ran through “Braceville and Windham.” Robbins goes on: Scott held up his left hand and counted the five items on his fingers, “then contrast it with the five points of Calvinism; and thus he made the Scripture order of the gospel so plain, that little boys could carry it home.”
Tried by the book

“They got their Bibles, and went to reading and searching for the truth. No word fell on the floor, or hit the wall—all was eagerly caught and tried by the book.”

J. G. Mitchell, on Scott at Warren, 1828 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 97
• The hearers checked the preacher against their own Bibles. Mitchell goes on: “They could do nothing against it; it was the simple gospel of Christ in its facts, and commands, and promises.” Elsewhere on the Reserve: “The Bibles were looked up, the dust brushed off, and the people began to read” (Hayden, p. 121).
Opinions, rather than faith

“I also discovered that I had never read the Scriptures, to form sentiments for myself. My religion consisted in opinions, rather than faith. I had been acting upon the credit system, and I was determined to abandon it at once.”

Jonas Hartzel, a farmer of Deerfield, in his own account · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 315
• A hearer using Campbell’s distinction for himself. Next: “We now began to read the Bible as we had never read it before.” Their study group of every sect: “No doctrinal standard was appealed to. All human authorities were ignored. The Bible was our book; Jesus Christ and his apostles were our umpire” (pp. 318–319).
A new book

“It was easily perceived the book was to be read like other books… From that time the Bible was studied as a new book, and oh, what a change it made! It is better remembered and felt than told.”

William Hayden, in his own words · William Baxter, Life of Elder Walter Scott (1874), pp. 198–199
• At a preachers’ meeting in New Lisbon, on “the true principles of interpretation”: “first, find who speaks, who it is spoken to, what is the subject, what is the object, and what is the context.” Then: “every diligent student of it could be a self-taught disciple.” Campbell’s method, in a lay preacher’s mouth.
The question
1.How did they unite around the Bible?
2.What made Scott’s preaching so compelling?
3.How could the Campbells embrace a Universalist?
4.What were all these people doing with the Bible?
Farmers, diarists, lay preachers. What were they doing?
Our questions
1.How did they unite around the Bible?
2.What made Scott’s preaching so compelling?
3.How could the Campbells embrace a Universalist?
4.What were all these people doing with the Bible?
Our questions so far. To answer them, a detour, through a Wright.
Another Wright

The accuser at Warren was a
Dr. Wright.

A small joke on the way. Two centuries later, another Wright is read all over the Churches of Christ, and here, and he reads the Bible the way Scott read it to Raines: as a story, in acts.
Two centuries later

N. T. Wright

Bishop of Durham (2003–2010); New Testament scholar at St Andrews and Oxford. Read across the Churches of Christ, and here at Otter Creek. Held over from Chapter 7: how Wright reads Scripture.
1 of 4

Wright is a historian.
He reads the Bible as a story.

The first of four things Wright does that Campbell did. Each pair: Wright, then one click for Campbell.
What God has done
Wright

“The historian has to plunge into the real world… in order to find out what it is in fact that God has sovereignly done…”

N. T. Wright, “The Meanings of History,” Journal of Analytic Theology 6 (2018), p. 22
Campbell

“Fact means something done.… That God exists, is a truth, but not a fact; that he created the heavens and the earth, is a fact and a truth.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), p. 115
Wright’s history and Campbell’s fact are the same thing: what God did. Campbell goes on: “The work of redemption is a system of works, or deeds, on the part of Heaven… the most splendid series of moral facts which man or angel ever saw” (p. 116). Raines: Scott preached Hebrews 11, faith as a story of deeds, and “here I virtually surrendered.”
Wright’s parable

“Suppose there exists a Shakespeare play whose fifth act had been lost.”

N. T. Wright, “How Can the Bible Be Authoritative?” (Laing Lecture, 1989), Vox Evangelica 21 (1991), p. 18
• He goes on: the first four acts are so rich that the play ought to be staged; rather than write a fifth act once for all, give the parts to experienced actors “who would immerse themselves in the first four acts, and in the language and culture of Shakespeare and his time, and who would then be told to work out a fifth act for themselves.” “The first four acts, existing as they did, would be the undoubted ‘authority’ for the task in hand.”
The five acts

Wright’s play

1. Creation
2. Fall
3. Israel
4. Jesus
5. The church: the New Testament its first scene, and we are on stage.
Five clicks. Laing Lecture, p. 19: “the possibility of seeing the five acts as follows: (1) Creation; (2) Fall; (3) Israel; (4) Jesus. The New Testament would then form the first scene in the fifth act, giving hints as well (Rom 8; 1 Cor 15; parts of the Apocalypse) of how the play is supposed to end.” Note 1 Corinthians 15: Raines’s chapter. Campbell’s acts: the Patriarchal, the Jewish, the Christian ages (Sermon on the Law, 1816; “the star-light… the moonlight… the sun-light of the moral world,” Christian Baptist, 1828).
In acts
Wright

“The Old Testament has the authority that an earlier act of the play would have, no more, no less.”

N. T. Wright, “How Can the Bible Be Authoritative?” (Laing Lecture, 1989), Vox Evangelica 21 (1991), p. 19
Campbell

“The first act of the great drama closes with the Deluge.”

Alexander Campbell’s Christian Baptist 6 (Dec. 1, 1828), “The Patriarchal Age.—No. V,” p. 118 (unsigned)
Raines’s third night: “I certainly did not know the difference between the old covenant and the new… I made of them a chaos.” Scott put the acts in order. Campbell’s serial on the ages ran in his paper the very months of the Raines story; Babel closes the second act, Abraham begins “a new chapter.” Rule 2: “Is he a Patriarch, a Jew, or a Christian?”
2 of 4

He pushes back on the creeds:
they divorce us from the text.

Not that they are false. They are incomplete as narrative.
Distilled
Wright

“…some of Christianity’s Great Traditions have slipped their moorings and floated off into the blue sky of speculation…”

N. T. Wright, “The Meanings of History,” Journal of Analytic Theology 6 (2018), p. 20
Campbell

“Some of those dogmas may be metaphysically true, but they are distilled truths. They have come from the Calvinistic or Arminian distillery.”

Alexander Campbell, Christian Baptist 2 (March 7, 1825), p. 151
Neither says the creeds are false: Campbell, “may be metaphysically true”; Wright’s example is Chalcedon, whose abstract terms “do not do justice to the vivid figure of the four Gospels” (Chadwick, quoted p. 20). Wright also: the Bible is not “creeds—lists of things to be believed” (Laing Lecture, p. 9). Raines: Scott said his Universalism “was a philosophy, as was Calvinism, Arminianism, etc., and no part of Christianity.”
3 of 4

He pushes back on atonement theories
that leave the story behind.

Wright, then Campbell on his own first great sermon.
The atonement
Wright

“Theories of atonement do not need to be superimposed on an abstract narrative about Jesus, as has so often been attempted. They grow out of the real-life Jesus stories we already have.”

N. T. Wright, The Day the Revolution Began (2016), p. 193
Campbell

“It was rather a youthful performance… Its views of the atonement are rather commercial than evangelical.”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger (1846), on his Sermon on the Law (1816), p. 493
Wright’s line: checked in Micah’s ebook (2026-11-04), not yet against a text in the database; recheck before class. Campbell reprinted the 1816 sermon thirty years on, unchanged, and flagged its atonement as a transaction (commercial) rather than the gospel (evangelical). That sermon got him tried for heresy by the Redstone Baptists: the young Campbell had his own Warren.
4 of 4

He points us to the renewal of all things,
and invites us to live in that story.

The last of the four.
The renewal of all things
Wright

“The point about new creation is that it is the renewal of this world, not the substitution of another one.”

N. T. Wright, “The Meanings of History,” Journal of Analytic Theology 6 (2018), p. 19
Campbell

“It shall have for its object the developement, and introduction of that political and religious order of society called THE MILLENNIUM…”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger 1 (1830), prospectus
The Harbinger began in January 1830, the year of Raines’s letter. The prospectus goes on: “which will be the consummation of that ultimate amelioration of society proposed in the Christian Scriptures.” Chapter 7’s theme: God’s future, lived now.
Living in the story
Wright

“The church would then live under the ‘authority’ of the extant story, being required to offer something between an improvisation and an actual performance of the final act.”

N. T. Wright, “How Can the Bible Be Authoritative?” (Laing Lecture, 1989), Vox Evangelica 21 (1991), p. 19
Campbell

“The fact, or the thing said to be done, produces the change in the frame of mind.”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), p. 122
Wright goes on: “And that is the task of the whole church. Need I say, not merely of the professional caste within it” (p. 27). Campbell’s chain: “fact, testimony, faith, and feeling” (p. 122), then action; the facts are “a moral seal or archetype” that draws God’s image on the soul (p. 116). Raines, 1830: “The facts of the New Testament will conquer the world. They have conquered me.”
The question
1.How did they unite around the Bible?
2.What made Scott’s preaching so compelling?
3.How could the Campbells embrace a Universalist?
4.What were all these people doing with the Bible?
5.Why is Wright popular among us?
The sub-question, asked after the pairs, and the storytelling trick: answer this one, and it frames the answer to the others. Answer, next slide.
Why Wright is popular among us

Both point us to
the power of the story.

The answer to question 6. We are drawn to Wright because he points where Campbell pointed: the story of Scripture, read whole, read as history, with power of its own to change us. Historian and story; past the creeds; past the atonement theories; into the renewal of all things. Campbell’s heirs kept his rules and lost his story; Wright gives it back.
Back to Warren

Back to Warren:
what Campbell said.

With Wright’s frame in hand: the Friday sermon, and the rule behind the vote.
The Friday sermon, as Hayden heard it

Three kinds of thing

Knowledge: what one has seen and heard for oneself. The apostles knew Jesus.
Faith: the facts reported to us, received on their testimony.
Opinion: everything else. “The fruitful source of all the schism.”
Three clicks. Hayden’s summary of Campbell’s sermon on Romans 14:1, pp. 164–165: “1st. Matters of knowledge — personal knowledge; 2d. The things of faith, the facts reported to us, which we accept on testimony; 3d. Matters of opinion.” “The apostles knew the gospel to be true, and none but they stood on this high ground of knowledge.” “As the facts of the gospel are always one and invariable… the faith of all persons is a unit. The important conclusion was thus reached, that Christians are not divided on the faith.” Opinion “was the fruitful source of all the schism which checkers, disgraces, and weakens the Christian profession.”
The rule

“Faith stands on testimony. No testimony, no faith.”

Campbell’s Friday sermon, in Hayden’s summary, p. 164
• Hayden goes on: “Testimony is delivered by witnesses. Christ’s apostles are his witnesses… Our faith in Christ is founded on the testimony of his witnesses… ‘Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God’; Rom. x: 17.” Hayden’s words, summarizing; not Campbell verbatim.
Applied to Raines

“…It could never be considered a matter of belief, since there was no testimony to render it such.”

Robert Richardson, Memoirs of Alexander Campbell, vol. 2 (1870), p. 245 (summarizing Campbell at Warren)
• Richardson: Raines’ view “could be regarded as nothing but an opinion, since there was not a passage anywhere in the writings of prophets or apostles affirming it.” Campbell then proposed that Raines “should express his willingness to preach the gospel as the apostles preached it, and to retain his opinions as private property in harmony with the principles of the Reformation.”
Alexander Campbell, in his own words

“If a person say such is his private opinion, let him have it as his private opinion; but lay no stress upon it; and if it be a wrong private opinion, it will die a natural death much sooner than if you attempt to kill it.”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger (1830), “Millennium.—No. II”, p. 147
• Written in 1830, telling this very story. Before it: “And will you receive a Universalist too? No; not as a Universalist. If a man, professing Universalist opinions, should apply for admission, we will receive him, if he will consent to use and apply all the Bible phrases in their plain reference to the future state of men and angels.” And of the essay’s whole argument: “We do not ask them to give up their opinions—we ask them only not to impose them upon others” (p. 145).
Two ways of reading

Raines, before and after

Before: a verse as proof. “The scrap.” The covenants a “hotch-potch,” “a chaos.”
Scott: the whole chapter. The covenants in order. The story of faith.
Two clicks. Same Bible, same man. What changed was the unit of reading: not the verse, the story.
Like any other book

“The words and sentences of the Bible are to be translated, interpreted, and understood according to the same code of laws and principles of interpretation by which other ancient writings are translated and understood…”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), “Rules of Interpretation,” p. 16
• He goes on: “for when God spoke to man in his own language, he spoke as one person converses with another.” Rule 1: “consider first the historical circumstances of the book”: the order, title, author, date, place and occasion. Rule 2: “observe who it is that speaks, and under what dispensation he officiates.”
Campbell’s rule

“In reading the historical and epistolary parts of the sacred writings, begin at the beginning and follow the writer in the train of his own thoughts and reasonings to the end of the subject on which he writes, irrespective of chapters and verses.”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger (1846), “Tracts for the People,” No. III, p. 22
• On the same page: dividing the Bible into chapters and verses has given it “the appearance of a book of proverbs.” Rule 2 of his rules of interpretation: “observe who it is that speaks, and under what dispensation he officiates. Is he a Patriarch, a Jew, or a Christian?” (Christian System, p. 16).
Campbell: a book of facts

“The Bible is a book of facts, not of opinions, theories, abstract generalities, nor of verbal definitions… History is therefore the plan pursued in both Testaments…”

Alexander Campbell, The Christian System (1839), p. 19
• In full: “It is a book of awful facts, grand and sublime beyond description. These facts reveal God and man… The meaning of the Bible facts is the true biblical doctrine. History is therefore the plan pursued in both Testaments; for testimony has primarily to do with faith, and reasoning with the understanding.” History and prophecy “make up exactly four-fifths of all the volumes of inspiration.” And: “Fact means something done” (p. 115). A book of deeds, a story; and its facts are received on testimony. That is the Warren sermon.
Raines

The rest
of the story.

In Raines’s own words, forty years on and two years on.
Forty years later

“Had they attempted to brow-beat me I might have been ruined forever. But treating me kindly, at the same time that they convinced me that my opinion, whether true or false, dwindled into nothingness in comparison with the faith of the gospel, redeemed me.”

Aylett Raines, recalling it in 1868 · A. S. Hayden, Early History of the Disciples in the Western Reserve (1875), p. 169
• Before it: “I was dealt with, and my case managed, by Bro. Campbell and all the chief brethren in very great kindness and wisdom.” After: “I became a day and night preacher of the gospel, and my mind becoming absorbed in this vast work, the opinion faded, and in ten months was numbered with all my former errors” (pp. 169–170; a page break falls in that sentence).
Two years later

“The facts of the New Testament will conquer the world. They have conquered me, and are now conquering thousands of others.”

Aylett Raines, letter to Campbell, Cincinnati, April 13, 1830 · Millennial Harbinger (1830), “Millennium.—No. II”, p. 149
• Checked by eye in the scan (“con quered” split across a line). The letter: “I wish to inform you that my ‘Restorationist’ sentiments have been slowly and imperceptibly erased from my mind, by the ministry of Paul and Peter… After my immersion, I brought my mind, as much as I possibly could, like a blank surface, to the ministry of the New Institution” (pp. 148–149). And: “My former associates persecute me, I would say, most cruelly.”
To Thomas Campbell

“I am strongly disposed to reciprocate the kindness of that beloved brother, by declaring, that, if I were Timothy, father Campbell should, in preference to any man, be my Paul.”

Aylett Raines, letter, 1830 · Millennial Harbinger (1830), “Millennium.—No. II”, p. 149
• “You will not call this flattery. It is a warm sentimental effusion of my heart.” Campbell printed the letter as proof of “the wisdom of the course pursued.” His own comment on his reasoning at Warren: “I urged this course from the conviction that, if these opinions were not agitated nor discussed, the ancient gospel would cause them to wither away. This was my philosophy then” (p. 148).
Campbell’s lesson

“Reason and experience unite their testimony in assuring us that, in the same proportion as individuals labor to be of one opinion, they disagree.”

Alexander Campbell, Millennial Harbinger (1830), “Millennium.—No. II”, p. 149
• He goes on: “The greater the emphasis laid upon opinions, the more rapidly they generate. The nearest approaches to a unity of opinion which I have ever witnessed, have appeared in those societies in which no effort was made to be of one opinion; in which they allowed the greatest liberty of opinion, and in which they talked more and boasted more of the glory and majesty of the great facts, the wonderful works of God’s loving kindness.” Honest notes: the terms were that Raines not teach his opinion; a minority nearly split the Association, and some would-be members walked away (Richardson II, p. 246).
The quiz, again

“Obey the gospel”

Which gospel? The story, read whole.
One click. Scott’s gospel was a story with points you could count on five fingers, preached a whole chapter at a time; Raines obeyed it before he had given up his opinion. The gospel to obey is the story, not a system about it.
Our questions
1.How did they unite around the Bible?
2.What made Scott’s preaching so compelling?
3.How could the Campbells embrace a Universalist?
4.What were all these people doing with the Bible?
5.Why is Wright popular among us?
All five, together. One answer serves them.
Today’s idea

The story does the work.

This is how Walter Scott can be so compelling.
This is how Alexander Campbell can embrace a Universalist.
This is how Stone-Campbell can unite on the Bible.
One idea, three clicks for its ramifications. Scott: four nights of whole chapters (1 Cor 1, 1 Cor 15, the two covenants, Hebrews 11); the story converted a man no argument could. Robbins: he convinced them “that God meant what he said.” Campbell: faith rests on the testimony of the story, “No testimony, no faith”; Raines’s Universalism was an opinion about what the story had not told, so it could be held “as private property.” And it was held kindly: Raines, “Had they attempted to brow-beat me I might have been ruined forever. But treating me kindly… redeemed me.” Stone-Campbell: Lexington, 1832, united on the story itself and left the readings free. Wright: the story is still going, and the whole church is in it.
◆ for discussion · Chapter 9

What is beautiful here? What do we carry forward?

Backup prompts (off the slide): Where do we still read the Bible as a book of proverbs, a verse at a time? What opinions do we hold as tests of fellowship? Who has been our Thomas Campbell, kind while we were wrong?
